# DnsLint v1.0.0

First release: a DNS health checkup tool, built from `app_template`,
on top of DnsResolver, FalconHTTP, RateThrottle, and MiniDatabase.
Runs live DNS queries against a submitted domain and reports missing
records, misconfigured email security, and TTL issues — with actual
decoded values (real IPv6 addresses, real mail server and nameserver
hostnames) rather than a plain pass/fail. Paired with a React
frontend for running and reading checks.

## Backend

- **`POST /api/check`** — the only endpoint. Takes `{"domain": "..."}`,
  runs eight checks against it (AAAA/MX/NS presence, SPF/DMARC/DKIM,
  A/MX TTL), and returns a `name`/`status`/`message` per check.
- **`GET /api/history?domain=...`** — returns the most recent past
  runs for a domain (newest first), each shaped the same as a
  `POST /api/check` response. Backed by `HistoryStore`
  (`backend/src/database/`), persisted via MiniDB.
- Real decoded values, not just pass/fail — AAAA shows the actual
  IPv6 address(es) found; MX/NS show the actual mail server/nameserver
  hostname(s), decoded straight out of DNS wire-format compression
  pointers; SPF/DMARC show the actual matched TXT record content.
  Every value found is listed (comma-joined), not truncated to
  "first + N more".
- Apex-domain-aware routing — MX, NS, DMARC, and MX-record TTL are
  checked against the domain's apex (a naive last-two-labels
  heuristic — `"b.com"` from `"a.b.com"`) regardless of what
  subdomain was submitted, since those records are apex-only concepts
  for any site. Everything else (AAAA, SPF, DKIM, A-record TTL) is
  checked against exactly what was submitted, since those can
  legitimately differ per subdomain.
- Domain input normalization — strips a leading scheme, path/query/
  fragment, and port from whatever's submitted, so a pasted URL like
  `"https://m.youtube.com/"` normalizes to `"m.youtube.com"` before
  being queried. The cleaned domain is what's echoed back in the
  response, not the raw input.
- DKIM checked best-effort against four common selectors (`google`,
  `selector1`, `default`, `k1`) — reports `warn`, not `fail`, when
  none match, since an unrecognized selector means "undetectable by
  this tool," not "missing."
- CORS enabled (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`) via FalconHTTP's
  `Cors` middleware — required since the frontend and backend are
  different origins even on `localhost`; safe here since the API
  takes no cookies/auth and returns nothing caller-specific.
- Rate limited — 60 requests/minute per client, keyed on
  `X-Forwarded-For`, via `RateLimiterMiddleware` wrapping
  RateThrottle's `RateLimiter`. Registered as a reference-capturing
  lambda rather than the middleware object directly, since
  `RateLimiterMiddleware` holds a `std::mutex` (via `RateLimiter`)
  and is therefore not copy-constructible, which FalconHTTP's
  `MiddlewareFn` requires.
- `QueryEngine` — one shared instance for the process's lifetime,
  doing raw UDP queries against a fixed recursive resolver
  (`8.8.8.8:53`, 2s timeout) via DnsPro's `Builder`/`Parser`. Not
  thread-safe against concurrent calls on its own; safe only because
  FalconHTTP is thread-per-connection and this is the sole route
  touching it.
- Transparent response caching, built into `QueryEngine` itself —
  every check benefits automatically, with no changes needed in any
  `checks/*.h` file. Cache duration is the shortest TTL among a
  response's answers (never cached longer than a real resolver would
  hold it), or a fixed 60s for a successful-but-empty answer set.
  Confirmed live: a repeat check against the same domain drops from
  ~140ms to ~2ms.
- `HistoryStore` persists every check run via MiniDB
  (`external/minidatabase`), with schema versioning done properly:
  a `meta` table tracks a real `schemaVersion`, and `runMigrations()`
  is genuine (if currently empty) machinery, not a promise. Verified
  by reading MiniDB's actual `Record::validate()` implementation (not
  just its doc comment): validation only checks a table's *declared*
  schema columns, never what's actually stored on a record -- so
  `check_runs` only declares `domain`/`checkedAt`, and the full nested
  `results` array is attached as a real field with zero schema
  declaration and zero migration code. Confirmed live across an
  actual process restart: history written before a `kill` was still
  correctly readable by a fresh process afterward, with the record-ID
  counter (`resyncNextRunId()`) correctly resuming above the highest
  ID already on disk -- no collisions, no lost data.
- Extended the vendored `DnsResolver` library itself (not just app
  code): added `ResourceRecord::rdataOffset` and made
  `Parser::parseName` public, so a compressed domain name embedded in
  a record's rdata (an MX exchange, an NS nsdname) can be decoded
  against the original message buffer — the library previously had no
  public way to do this. Covered by two new regression tests added to
  both of the library's test suites; full existing suite re-run
  afterward with no regressions (32/32 GoogleTest cases, 958/958
  custom-framework checks).

## Frontend

- Vite + React 19 + TypeScript, Tailwind v4 (CSS-first `@theme`
  tokens, no config file), React Router v7.
- Visual direction grounded in the subject itself rather than a
  generic dark-dashboard palette: router/switch status LEDs are
  literally green/amber-orange/red, and DNS tooling output (`dig`,
  `traceroute`) is monospace by nature — both borrowed on purpose.
  Space Grotesk for headlines, Manrope for body, JetBrains Mono for
  anything that's real DNS data.
- Checker page: a resolution-trace hop chain
  (`. → com → example.com`) that lights up sequentially while a check
  runs, standing in for a generic spinner; a summary panel with a
  signal-bars score and pass/warn/issue counts; a result list showing
  each check's real decoded value rather than an expandable generic
  definition.
- About page documents what each of the eight checks means, including
  an explicit note on DKIM's selector limitation.

## Tooling

- `docs/Doxyfile` retargeted (`PROJECT_NAME`/`PROJECT_BRIEF`) and
  verified against the real `backend/include`/`backend/src` — a full
  HTML doc site generates cleanly, correctly excluding
  `backend/external`.
- `README.md` and `.github/assets/` (banner, divider, back-to-top)
  retargeted from `app_template`'s scaffold — recolored from the
  template's cyan/violet/purple to DnsLint's own green/orange, and
  filled in with DnsLint-specific Features/Getting Started/Project
  Structure content in place of the template's placeholders.
- `.clang-format`/`.clang-tidy`, root `.gitignore`, `Dockerfile`
  (`BINARY_NAME`-parameterized), and the MIT `LICENSE` are inherited
  unmodified from `app_template` — not app-specific, nothing to
  retarget.

## CI

Inherited unmodified from `app_template`'s scaffold — none of these
workflows were authored or re-verified against DnsLint's actual
endpoints in this release:

- **Build** — Linux, GCC + Clang, Debug + Release.
- **Clang Format** / **Clang Tidy** — static analysis and formatting
  checks on `backend/include` and `backend/src`.
- **Sanitizers** — ASan+UBSan and TSan jobs; still boot-only smoke
  tests as of this release, with the template's own `TODO`s for real
  endpoint checks left unaddressed even though DnsLint now has one
  (`POST /api/check`) they could exercise.
- **Frontend** — lint + build for `frontend/`.
- **Docs** — Doxygen → GitHub Pages.
- **Release** — this workflow, publishing `.github/releases/<tag>.md`
  as the GitHub Release body on any `v*` tag push.
- **Dependabot** — weekly updates for GitHub Actions and `frontend/`
  npm dependencies.

Everything described in Backend/Frontend above was instead verified
locally: `cmake --build` against the real `external/` submodules,
`tsc -b` + `npm run build` for the frontend, `doxygen` for the docs,
and `DnsResolver`'s own test suites.

## Known limitations

- DKIM detection only covers four hardcoded selectors — a domain
  using any other selector shows as "not detected" rather than a
  definitive pass or fail.
- Apex-domain derivation is a naive last-two-labels heuristic, not a
  real Public Suffix List lookup — wrong for compound TLDs
  (`www.example.co.uk` reduces to `co.uk`, not `example.co.uk`).
- Recursive resolver only (a fixed `8.8.8.8:53`) — reflects what's
  currently propagated/cached, not necessarily a domain owner's very
  latest change; no authoritative-NS lookup path.
- Rate limiting is per-visitor only — nothing currently caps outbound
  query volume per submitted domain, so a burst of different domains
  from different visitors isn't throttled at the DNS-query level,
  only at the request level.
- No automated test suite for DnsLint's own backend or frontend
  (`checks/`, `routes/`, or any React component) — all verification
  in this release was manual, against a live running server. The
  regression tests added this release live in `DnsResolver`, a
  dependency, not this app.
- Sanitizer CI jobs (see CI above) still only verify the binary
  boots — not updated in this release to exercise the real
  `POST /api/check` path or its concurrency behavior.
- A handful of Doxygen `\brief` gaps surfaced by
  `WARN_IF_UNDOCUMENTED` (`main()`, a couple of
  `RateLimiterMiddleware.h` internals, `QueryResult`'s fields) —
  flagged, not yet filled in.
- No deployment config specific to DnsLint beyond the inherited
  `Dockerfile` — no live host set up as part of this release.
  `backend/data/` (where `HistoryStore` writes `dnslint.json`) MUST be
  a mounted persistent volume in any real deployment, not a path
  inside the container's own writable layer, or a redeploy silently
  wipes it — this is called out directly in `main.cpp`'s own comments,
  not left implicit.
- `kCurrentSchemaVersion` is `1` and nothing has migrated from a prior
  version yet in this release — `runMigrations()` exists and is
  documented, but its actual migration-writing path is unexercised
  until a real schema change happens.
- MiniDB has no auto-increment record IDs — `HistoryStore` tracks
  `nextRunId_` itself and re-derives it from the highest ID on disk at
  startup (`resyncNextRunId()`), rather than the library handling
  that.
- Response caching has no explicit size-based memory bound beyond its
  fixed entry-count LRU capacity (500 distinct (domain, RecordType)
  pairs by default) — fine at this scale, but not something that
  adapts to actual memory pressure.
